lead: Both readings open the doors of God's house to the nations. Paul announces the "mystery" that the Gentiles are fellow heirs with Israel. In the Gospel a Gentile centurion shows a faith that amazes Jesus, and Jesus foresees many coming "from east and west" to the banquet of the kingdom. Today the Church also remembers Sts Zechariah and Elizabeth, the parents of John the Baptist.

set: Ephesians 2 has just described how Christ broke down "the dividing wall" between Jews and Gentiles and made them one new people (2:14–16), "a holy temple in the Lord" (2:21). In chapter 3 Paul, writing as a prisoner, explains his own part in this plan.
str: v. 1: Paul, a prisoner for the sake of the Gentiles.
vv. 2–4: the grace given to him, and the mystery made known by revelation.
v. 5: hidden in former generations, now revealed by the Spirit.
v. 6: the content of the mystery: the Gentiles are fellow heirs.
kw: Literally "the management of a household". God runs his house according to a plan, and Paul is given a steward's task in it (v. 2).
Not a secret kept from people but God's plan, once hidden and now opened. Here its content is precise: Jews and Gentiles together in one body.
fellow heirs, members of the same body, sharers
Paul strings together three words beginning with "syn-", "together with". The Gentiles do not receive a second-class place; they share the same inheritance, the same body, the same promise.
vv: I Paul am a prisoner for Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles
Paul's chains are part of his mission. He was arrested in Jerusalem because he brought the gospel to the Gentiles (Acts 21:28; 22:21–22).
In former generations this mystery was not made known to humankind
The prophets had glimpsed that the nations would come to Zion (Isaiah 2:2–3), but the full form of the plan, one body in Christ, was revealed only after Easter.
that is, the Gentiles have become fellow heirs, members of the same body, and sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
The Gentiles are joined to the promise first made to Abraham. The Church does not replace Israel's hope; she is grafted into it (compare Romans 11:17–18).
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church is the new People of God, gathered from Jews and Gentiles and made one in the Spirit (Lumen Gentium 9). The same Council asks Christians to remember that the Church received the revelation of the Old Testament through the people of Israel (Nostra Aetate 4).

set: After the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7), Matthew presents ten mighty works of Jesus (chapters 8–9). The first three heal people on the edge of Israel's community: a leper, the servant of a Gentile officer, and a woman, Peter's mother-in-law. Capernaum, on the Sea of Galilee, was Jesus' base during his ministry.

A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. In Galilee he was probably in the service of Herod Antipas. Luke's account of the same event says that this man loved the Jewish people and built their synagogue (Luke 7:5).
str: vv. 8–9: "I am not worthy"; the soldier's understanding of authority.
vv. 10–12: Jesus' amazement, and the saying about east and west.
v. 13: "let it be done for you according to your faith."
kw: An officer over about a hundred men. He knows what authority is: a word given, and it is done.
The Greek word can mean a child or a servant. Matthew's word is warm: this master cares deeply about one of his household.
vv: Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof; but only speak the word, and my servant will be healed.
A Jew who entered a Gentile house could become ritually unclean. The centurion spares Jesus this, and he believes that Jesus' word works at a distance, as God's word does.
Truly I tell you, in no one in Israel have I found such faith.
Only twice in the Gospels is Jesus said to be amazed: at this man's faith and at the unbelief of his own town (Mark 6:6).
many will come from east and west and will eat with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven

An echo of the prophets who saw the nations gathered for God's banquet (Isaiah 25:6). The warning of v. 12 about "the heirs of the kingdom" is not a judgment on the Jewish people as such; it warns everyone, Christians included, that belonging is not enough without faith.
ch: St Augustine says that by calling himself unworthy, the centurion became worthy to receive Christ, not under his roof but into his heart (in substance). The Roman liturgy places his words on the lips of every communicant before Holy Communion, and the Catechism quotes them in its teaching on the Eucharist (CCC 1386).

rite: Sts Zechariah and Elizabeth, remembered today, were "righteous before God" (Luke 1:6). Elizabeth was the first to greet Mary as "the mother of my Lord" (Luke 1:43). Like the centurion, they lived by trust in God's word, and Zechariah learned in silence to believe what the angel promised.
study: Ephesians 3:6 uses three "together" words. Who in my parish or neighbourhood feels like an outsider, and how can I help them share fully in the life of the Church?
The centurion believes that Jesus' word is enough (Matthew 8:8). Where do I need to trust the Lord's word without seeing the result at once?
